# Responsibilities and execution order

Member 1 performs all data cleaning and analysis-input preparation. Later members consume named objects without repeating capping, scaling or sample splitting. Keep the small chunks and run them in order on the first pass.

| Member | Responsibility | First chunk | Last chunk | Main handoff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cleaning, derived fields, clustering inputs, train/validation data and exports | `setup` | `export-clean-csv` | `bank_clean`, prepared copies, clean CSV and RDS |
| 2 | Exploratory and bivariate analysis | `clv-correlations` | `young-correlation` | Associations and tests using original numeric values |
| 3 | K-means comparison, selection and sensitivity analysis | `check-cluster-inputs` | `sensitivity-no-capping` | `km_final`, `bank_clustered` |
| 4 | Cluster profiling and interpretation | `selected-clusters` | `cluster-scatter` | Profiles using original numeric values |
| 5 | Regression fitting, interpretation, diagnostics and validation | `check-regression-inputs` | `age-errors` | Coefficients, errors and limitations |
| 6 | Recommendations, integration and final outputs | `profit-ranking` | `session` | Actions and analytical results |

**Dependencies:** Run Member 1 first in a fresh R session. Members 2, 3 and 5 can then run independently. Member 4 also needs Member 3; Member 6 needs the relevant analytical results. Full Knit still follows members 1–6. Member 3 creates `bank_clustered` without adding Cluster to `bank_clean`. Member numbers refer to responsibilities, not the assignment's Part numbers.

**Boundary:** Cleaning and input preparation belong to Member 1. Cluster fitting, segment names, predictions, residuals, Cook's distance and the temporary influence-sensitivity refit depend on model results and stay in their analysis blocks. Diagnostics do not delete rows from the main data.

# Before starting: a concrete assignment plan

This notebook follows the new `assignment requirement.docx` for the full Assignment 3 workflow. The earlier cleaning checklist is no longer the requirements source. This is an analysis and presentation preparation notebook, not a finished slide deck. The Chinese and English versions use identical code, seeds and analytical choices; run either version.

The business questions are: which segments generate more current profit and have higher recorded lifetime value? Which characteristics are associated with recorded CLV? Which actions should the bank test? The proposed approach is **K-means plus linear regression of CLV**. The assignment permits either regression or CART, and either CLV or Yield; multiple primary models are unnecessary.

Run the small chunks in order on the first pass because later chunks depend on earlier objects. Each section explains what to do, why, and what to read. A few simple `for` loops repeat calculations; no custom R functions are defined.

| Stage | Work to complete | Completion evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Part 1 | Types, zero income, outliers, age consistency, bivariate CLV analysis | Tables, plots and treatment decisions, including customers under 30 |
| Part 2 | Inputs, scaling, k=2–8 comparison, selection and naming | Sizes and means/proportions for every variable, including Yield and CLV |
| Part 3 | Model choice, regression, coefficients, diagnostics and validation | Associations with recorded CLV, prediction errors and limitations |
| Part 4 | Combine profiles and model evidence | At least three actions linked to specific segments and model results |
| Part 5 | Plan the presentation and appendices | Ten main slides, ten minutes of speaking points and Q&A |

**Source priority:** the complete assignment defines the task; course materials guide the method. The closing example in the W7 lecture mentions Yield, but the complete assignment permits CLV and/or Yield, so this proposal selects CLV. Some solution PDFs retain older lab numbers in their headings; references below follow the supplied folders and filenames.

**Your decision:** this notebook provides a complete proposed solution with executed interpretations, including four segments and CLV regression. The assignment requires students to make the final model choice. Read the results and be able to explain the choices in your own words.

## Course map and taught-versus-additional labels

**Covered** means the supplied materials provide evidence. **Adapted** means the method was covered but is applied to different variables or code here. **Additional** means the specific procedure was not located in the supplied materials; it does not imply the instructor never mentioned it. The available folders are W3, W4, W6, W7, W8 and W9.

| Source | Application here | Status |
|---|---|---|
| W3 `Week 3 Solution.pdf`, Exercises 1, 2, 4 | Means/medians, distributions, implausible values | Covered |
| W4 `Lab 4 Solution.pdf`, Exercise 1B; W4 Bivariate Analysis, pp. 6–8 | Welch t-test for a binary group and numeric outcome; proportions | Covered |
| W6 `Week 6 Solution.pdf`, Exercises 1A–1C | Correlations, boxplots, group comparisons and measurement levels | Covered |
| W7 `Week 7 Solution.pdf`, Exercises 1–4; lecture slides 15–21, 24–34 | scale, kmeans, silhouette, profiles, names and interpretation | Covered |
| W8 `Week 8 Solution.pdf`, Exercises 1–3; lecture slides 21, 27–29 | lm, summary, diagnostics, VIF and standardized coefficients | Covered; the base R VIF calculation is additional code |
| W9 `Week 9 CART Analysis.pdf`, Exercise 2 | Training/validation split and RMSE, adapted to regression | Adapted |
| Explicitly labelled additions below | P99 capping, sampled silhouette, duplicate checks, sensitivity analysis, MAE and mean baseline | Additional; not presented as copied classroom code |

There is no need to use every statistical test taught. Without observed future profit, a comparison of younger and older customers cannot establish that younger customers' CLV is underestimated. It only compares recorded CLV.

Integer storage does not imply identical measurement levels. Products and transactions are counts. Age is recorded in years and used numerically. Cat_Age is ordinal, not age in years. Yield may be negative; CLV is derived from an unknown formula.

Covered: W3/W6 checks for implausible values. The complete assignment defines products 0–5, age 18–99 and age codes 1–6. Unobserved product count 0 or age code 1 is not automatically invalid.

```{r missing-range}
  Invalid_transactions = sum(raw_data$No_Trans < 0 | raw_data$No_Trans %% 1 != 0),

range_checks
```

## 1.17 Quantify outlier flags

Additional implementation: count flags using the usual 1.5 × IQR boxplot rule and report the 99th percentile. Screening does not imply deletion.

```{r outlier-table}
outlier_table <- data.frame()
for (variable in numeric_vars) {
  x <- bank_clean[[variable]]
  q1 <- unname(quantile(x, 0.25))
  q3 <- unname(quantile(x, 0.75))
  lower <- q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
  upper <- q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
  outlier_table <- rbind(outlier_table, data.frame(
    Variable = variable, Minimum = min(x), Maximum = max(x),
    P99 = unname(quantile(x, 0.99)),
    Flagged = sum(x < lower | x > upper)))
}
outlier_table
```

### Treatment decisions and reasons

Retain all customer records and original outcomes. Negative Yield is explicitly permitted. Four/five products and plausible old ages are not errors. High income, transaction counts and CLV may be genuine. W3/W6 remove or recode impossible ages; that is not a rule to delete every statistical outlier.

W7 warns that K-means is sensitive to extremes. Cap the top 1% of Income and No_Trans only in a clustering copy, then standardize. **The P99 threshold is an additional analytical choice, not a course requirement.** Compare with an uncapped solution later. Never cap the original Yield or CLV. Regression starts separately from the original data, not from the clustering copy.

## 1.18 Check age categories

Adapt W4 cross-tabulation and W7 grouped summaries. Observe the boundaries before checking each row; these inferred boundaries are not an official dictionary supplied by the assignment.

```{r age-mapping}
aggregate(Age ~ Cat_Age, data = bank_clean, FUN = min)
aggregate(Age ~ Cat_Age, data = bank_clean, FUN = max)
expected_age_group <- cut(bank_clean$Age, breaks = c(17, 35, 50, 64, 79, 99),
                          labels = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6))
table(Recorded = bank_clean$Cat_Age, Expected = expected_age_group, useNA = "ifany")
sum(as.character(bank_clean$Cat_Age) != as.character(expected_age_group))
```

Observed age bands are 18–35, 36–50, 51–64, 65–79 and 80–99, with consistent mapping. Use Age in models and Cat_Age in profiles. Including both repeats age information and may cause multicollinearity in regression. The specific cut-based consistency check is additional code.


## 1.19 Data objects and handoff rules

Member 1 now prepares every later analysis input. raw_data remains untouched. bank_clean preserves original numeric values while changing the categorical type and adding helper fields. Later analyses do not add cluster results to either object.

| Object | Purpose | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `bank_clean`, `young_data` | Original-value exploration and age comparisons | Member 2 |
| `cluster_data`, `cluster_scaled` | Capped four-variable copy and standardized matrix | Member 3 |
| `without_income`, `uncapped_scaled` | Inputs for two sensitivity analyses | Member 3 |
| `silhouette_rows`, `silhouette_distances` | Fixed evaluation sample and distances | Member 3 |

Member 3 later creates bank_clustered by adding cluster labels to a copy of bank_clean. Member 4 profiles this copy using original numeric values. Preparation moves earlier; the analytical choices remain the same.


## 1.20 Create helper fields and the younger-customer subset

These fields encode explicit rules, not predictions. Under_30 uses Age < 30; loss and zero-income flags support Member 4 proportions. Preserve source row order. Income_group was already created during the zero-income check.

```{r prepare-analysis-groups}
bank_clean$Under_30 <- factor(ifelse(bank_clean$Age < 30, "Under 30", "30 and above"),
                              levels = c("Under 30", "30 and above"))
bank_clean$Loss_flag <- bank_clean$Yield < 0
bank_clean$Zero_income_flag <- bank_clean$Income == 0
young_data <- bank_clean[bank_clean$Age < 30, ]
table(bank_clean$Under_30)
c(Loss_records = sum(bank_clean$Loss_flag),
  Zero_income_records = sum(bank_clean$Zero_income_flag))
```

## 1.21 Choose clustering inputs

Covered: W7 Exercises 1/2. Use Tot_Prod for relationship breadth, Income for income level, No_Trans for activity, and Age for life stage. As required, exclude Yield and CLV. Do not duplicate Age with Cat_Age. Inspect input correlations for redundant information.

```{r cluster-inputs}
cluster_vars <- c("Tot_Prod", "Income", "No_Trans", "Age")
cluster_data <- bank_clean[cluster_vars]
round(cor(cluster_data), 3)
```

## 1.22 Cap the clustering copy

Additional: cap only the two variables used in distance calculations. P99 is not an estimate of a true value. Calculate thresholds from this file rather than copying the earlier checklist. pmin keeps values below the limit unchanged.

```{r cluster-capping}
income_cap <- unname(quantile(cluster_data$Income, 0.99))
transaction_cap <- unname(quantile(cluster_data$No_Trans, 0.99))
cluster_data$Income <- pmin(cluster_data$Income, income_cap)
cluster_data$No_Trans <- pmin(cluster_data$No_Trans, transaction_cap)
data.frame(Variable = c("Income", "No_Trans"),
           Cap = c(income_cap, transaction_cap),
           Changed = c(sum(bank_clean$Income > income_cap),
                       sum(bank_clean$No_Trans > transaction_cap)))
```

## 1.23 Standardize inputs

Covered: W7 scale. Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation because units affect Euclidean distances. Scaling does not remove correlation or establish equal business importance.

```{r cluster-scaling}
cluster_scaled <- scale(cluster_data)
round(colMeans(cluster_scaled), 6)
apply(cluster_scaled, 2, sd)
```


## 1.24 Prepare clustering inputs without Income

Additional: prepare an income-exclusion sensitivity check. Keep the capped transaction input from the main clustering copy, omit Income, then standardize. Member 3 fits and compares the alternative model.

```{r prepare-no-income}
without_income <- scale(cluster_data[c("Tot_Prod", "No_Trans", "Age")])
colnames(without_income)
dim(without_income)
```


## 1.25 Prepare clustering inputs without capping

Additional: standardize the four original-value inputs from bank_clean without capping. Keep the main copy unchanged. This supports checking how P99 capping affects membership.

```{r prepare-no-capping}
uncapped_scaled <- scale(bank_clean[cluster_vars])
round(colMeans(uncapped_scaled), 6)
apply(uncapped_scaled, 2, sd)
```

## 1.26 Prepare silhouette evaluation sample

Silhouette is covered in W7; **sampling it is additional**. A 10,000-customer distance matrix is large, so evaluate on the same fixed 2,000-customer sample for each k. K-means still fits all customers. Report a sample-based approximation, not an exact full-data silhouette.

```{r silhouette-sample}
set.seed(700)
silhouette_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(bank_clean)), size = 2000)
silhouette_distances <- dist(cluster_scaled[silhouette_rows, ])
```

## 1.27 Split training and validation data

Adapted from W9 Exercise 2: training/validation and RMSE. Use a reproducible random 70/30 split; this random split adapts the lab, which uses consecutive rows. Develop and diagnose on training data, then evaluate on validation. Without IDs, distinct records cannot be guaranteed to represent distinct customers.

```{r train-validation}
set.seed(700)
train_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(raw_data)), size = floor(0.7 * nrow(raw_data)))
train_data <- bank_clean[train_rows, ]
validation_data <- bank_clean[-train_rows, ]
c(Training = nrow(train_data), Validation = nrow(validation_data))
```


## 1.28 Prepare a training-only standardized regression copy

Covered concept: W8 standardized coefficients, implemented with scale. Split 70/30 first, then standardize the training outcome and three predictors using training rows only. The main regression still uses original-value train_data. This separate copy only supports coefficient comparison, not validation predictions. No validation means or standard deviations enter this transformation.

```{r prepare-standardized-training}
standardized_train <- as.data.frame(scale(train_data[c("CLV", "Tot_Prod", "No_Trans", "Age")]))
round(colMeans(standardized_train), 6)
apply(standardized_train, 2, sd)
```


## 1.29 Check the prepared handoff data

Check that original values are preserved, clustering excludes outcomes, and training/validation rows are separate. If a check fails, correct Member 1 before continuing.

```{r preparation-checks}
stopifnot(identical(raw_data, read.csv(data_path)))
stopifnot(nrow(bank_clean) == nrow(raw_data))
stopifnot(identical(bank_clean[numeric_vars], raw_data[numeric_vars]))
stopifnot(is.ordered(bank_clean$Cat_Age))
stopifnot(!"Cluster" %in% names(bank_clean))
stopifnot(!any(c("Yield", "CLV", "Cat_Age") %in% colnames(cluster_scaled)))
stopifnot(nrow(cluster_scaled) == nrow(bank_clean))
stopifnot(nrow(train_data) + nrow(validation_data) == nrow(bank_clean))
stopifnot(length(intersect(rownames(train_data), rownames(validation_data))) == 0)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(cluster_scaled)), all(is.finite(as.matrix(standardized_train))))
c(Clean_rows = nrow(bank_clean), Clustering_rows = nrow(cluster_scaled),
  Training_rows = nrow(train_data), Validation_rows = nrow(validation_data))
```


## 1.30 Save the prepared objects for handoff

Additional file management: CSV is convenient for viewing and sharing but cannot retain ordered-factor metadata, scaling attributes or multiple objects. Also save a simple RDS list. Read it with `prepared <- readRDS(...)`, then access objects such as `prepared$cluster_scaled`. This is file storage, not a custom function. Each language uses a new output folder, preserving existing results.

```{r save-prepared-objects}
prep_output_dir <- "outputs/study_en_updated/member1"
dir.create(prep_output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(bank_clean = bank_clean, young_data = young_data,
             numeric_vars = numeric_vars, cluster_vars = cluster_vars,
             cluster_data = cluster_data, cluster_scaled = cluster_scaled,
             without_income = without_income, uncapped_scaled = uncapped_scaled,
             income_cap = income_cap, transaction_cap = transaction_cap,
             silhouette_rows = silhouette_rows, silhouette_distances = silhouette_distances,
             train_rows = train_rows, train_data = train_data,
             validation_data = validation_data, standardized_train = standardized_train),
        file.path(prep_output_dir, "Member1_prepared_objects_updated.rds"))
```

This is the last chunk of Member 1. Export 10,000 rows and 11 columns: the seven original fields plus Income_group, Under_30, Loss_flag and Zero_income_flag. No rows are removed, no values are imputed, and original numeric values stay unchanged. The CSV contains no cluster labels, capped values or z-scores. Income_group uses Zero/Positive; the two flags use TRUE/FALSE.

After reading the CSV, restore the ordered age category with `factor(clean_data$Cat_Age, levels = 1:6, ordered = TRUE)`; restore the helper-group levels as defined above when needed. Use the preceding RDS to preserve R types and all prepared matrices. Later analysis chunks use the current in-memory objects and do not need to reload the CSV.

```{r export-clean-csv}

clean_csv_path <- file.path(prep_output_dir, "Group_presentation_cleaned_updated.csv")
write.csv(member1_cleaned, file = clean_csv_path, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Member 2 — Exploratory and bivariate analysis

**Start of responsibility block.**

## 2.1 Bivariate relationships with CLV

Covered: W6 correlations and W8 Exercise 1. Use scatterplots and Pearson correlations for numeric pairs. Exclude category codes from numeric correlations. Correlation is not causation and may be influenced by extremes.

```{r clv-correlations}
correlation_table <- round(cor(bank_clean[numeric_vars]), 3)
correlation_table
for (variable in c("Tot_Prod", "Income", "No_Trans", "Age", "Yield")) {
  plot(bank_clean[[variable]], bank_clean$CLV, xlab = variable, ylab = "CLV",
       main = paste("CLV and", variable), pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.15))
}
```

## 2.2 Test the linear association between age and CLV

Covered: W6 Exercise 1A. H0: population linear correlation is zero; H1: it is nonzero. Use a two-sided test. The overall correlation is about 0.054; a large sample can make a small association significant, so report magnitude as well as p-value.

```{r age-correlation-test}
cor.test(bank_clean$Age, bank_clean$CLV, alternative = "two.sided")
```

## 2.3 Describe the prepared under 30 group

Member 1 has prepared Under_30 and young_data using Age < 30. Summarise these objects here; Cat_Age=2 also includes ages 30–35. Report means and medians to distinguish typical values from the influence of extremes.

```{r young-summary}
table(bank_clean$Under_30)
aggregate(cbind(Income, No_Trans, Tot_Prod, Yield, CLV) ~ Under_30,
          data = bank_clean, FUN = mean)
aggregate(cbind(Income, No_Trans, Tot_Prod, Yield, CLV) ~ Under_30,
          data = bank_clean, FUN = median)
```

## 2.4 CLV boxplot and Welch comparison

Covered: W4 Exercise 1B. H0: the groups have equal mean recorded CLV; H1: they differ. Welch does not assume equal variances, but observations should be independent and means meaningful. Skewness and unknown sampling design limit inference.

```{r young-test}
boxplot(CLV ~ Under_30, data = bank_clean, xlab = "Age group", ylab = "Recorded CLV")
young_test <- t.test(CLV ~ Under_30, data = bank_clean)
young_test
```

## 2.5 Associations within younger customers

Adapted from W6 subgroup correlations. Overall and subgroup patterns can differ, so inspect younger customers separately.

```{r young-correlation}
round(cor(young_data[numeric_vars]), 3)
```

### Interpretation for Part 1

Mean recorded CLV is approximately $1,246 for customers under 30 and $2,079 for others. Younger customers also have lower mean Income, No_Trans and Yield. The CLV difference is statistically significant, but it does not establish underestimation. Lower CLV may reflect customer characteristics, the old formula's treatment of age, or both. Without observed future profits, relationship duration or the original formula, no justified upward correction can be calculated.

Income correlates with CLV at about 0.777 and Yield at about 0.562. This motivates investigating whether the formula used these variables, but correlation cannot identify the formula. Exclude Income and Yield from the main regression to reduce mechanical replication risk, while recognizing that omitted information can reduce fit. The remaining predictors may also have been used in the old formula.

**Member 2 block ends here.**

# Member 3 — K-means clustering and solution selection

**Start of responsibility block.**


## 3.1 Receive the clustering inputs from Member 1

Use cluster_scaled, the two sensitivity inputs and the fixed evaluation sample prepared by Member 1. Do not cap or scale again here. Check dimensions and columns, then fit and compare models. Input-choice rationale and transformation settings are documented in Member 1.

```{r check-cluster-inputs}
dim(cluster_scaled)
colnames(cluster_scaled)
stopifnot(nrow(cluster_scaled) == nrow(bank_clean))
stopifnot(nrow(without_income) == nrow(cluster_scaled),
          nrow(uncapped_scaled) == nrow(cluster_scaled))
```

## 3.2 Compare k=2 to 8

Covered: W7 loop, kmeans and nstart=25. Fix the seed for each k and allow more iterations. Save each solution for profiling without refitting.

```{r compare-k}
cluster_models <- list()
k_comparison <- data.frame()
for (k in 2:8) {
  set.seed(700)
  km <- kmeans(cluster_scaled, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
  cluster_models[[as.character(k)]] <- km
  silhouette_result <- silhouette(km$cluster[silhouette_rows], silhouette_distances)
  k_comparison <- rbind(k_comparison, data.frame(
    K = k, Silhouette = mean(silhouette_result[, 3]),
    Smallest_cluster = min(table(km$cluster)),
    Largest_cluster = max(table(km$cluster))))
}
k_comparison
```

## 3.3 Plot silhouette scores

Covered: W7. Higher is generally better, but consider sizes, profiles and actionability. Do not claim exceptionally clear natural segments in this dataset.

```{r silhouette-plot}
plot(k_comparison$K, k_comparison$Silhouette, type = "b",
     xlab = "Number of clusters", ylab = "Sample-based mean silhouette",
     main = "Compare K-means solutions")
```

## 3.4 Inspect original-scale profiles for every candidate

Covered: W7 Exercise 3. Profile original values, not z-scores or capped values. Print sizes and all numeric means for every k; the next chunk provides Cat_Age proportions. Yield and CLV are passive profiling variables.

```{r candidate-profiles}
for (k in 2:8) {
  cat("
Number of clusters:", k, "
")
  groups <- cluster_models[[as.character(k)]]$cluster
  print(table(groups))
  print(aggregate(bank_clean[numeric_vars], by = list(Cluster = groups), FUN = mean))
}
```

## 3.5 Age-category proportions for candidates

Covered: W4/W7 cross-tabulations. margin=1 gives percentages within each cluster. Category 1 has no observations; retain its zero column to show the complete coding.

```{r candidate-categories}
for (k in 2:8) {
  cat("
Number of clusters:", k, "
")
  groups <- cluster_models[[as.character(k)]]$cluster
  print(round(prop.table(table(groups, bank_clean$Cat_Age), margin = 1) * 100, 1))
}
```

### Why select four clusters?

k=2 has the highest sample silhouette, about 0.317, but primarily separates lower-activity from higher-activity customers. It mixes older and younger customers and does not distinguish active customers by product breadth. k=4 scores about 0.305, a reduction of about 0.013, while separating life stage and product breadth. k=3 scores about 0.291 and combines the two active segments. k=5–8 add groups and presentation complexity without exceeding the k=2 score.

Select k=4 as a **profile-based business compromise**, not the mathematical score winner. Each group contains at least 1,855 customers and can be explained within ten minutes. W7 describes scores between 0.26 and 0.50 as weak separation: overlap remains. These are descriptive segments in this sample, not proven permanent customer types.


## 3.6 Save the selected labels for handoff

Member 3 selects four groups after inspecting candidate profiles and saves the labels. Member 4 assigns names based on the profiles.

```{r select-final-clusters}
chosen_k <- 4
km_final <- cluster_models[[as.character(chosen_k)]]
bank_clustered <- bank_clean
bank_clustered$Cluster <- factor(km_final$cluster)
table(bank_clustered$Cluster)
```

## 3.7 Additional sensitivity: omit Income

Additional: ambiguous zero income motivates checking a solution without Income. Keep the same k and other preprocessing. Cluster numbers are arbitrary, so diagonal agreement is not an accuracy measure.

```{r sensitivity-no-income}
set.seed(700)
km_without_income <- kmeans(without_income, centers = 4, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
no_income_comparison <- table(Main = bank_clustered$Cluster, Without_income = km_without_income$cluster)
no_income_comparison
round(prop.table(no_income_comparison, 1), 3)
```

## 3.8 Additional sensitivity: no capping

Additional: assess the P99 choice. Use uncapped_scaled prepared by Member 1 and fit the same k without changing the main model. Inspect sizes and cross-tabulations, rather than choosing whichever result supports a preferred conclusion.

```{r sensitivity-no-capping}
set.seed(700)
km_uncapped <- kmeans(uncapped_scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
uncapped_comparison <- table(Main = bank_clustered$Cluster, Uncapped = km_uncapped$cluster)
uncapped_comparison
round(prop.table(uncapped_comparison, 1), 3)
table(km_uncapped$cluster)
```

### Interpreting sensitivity results

Without Income, about 97.9%, 84.3%, 94.8% and 85.2% of main-solution Clusters 1–4 fall into their respective closest-matching alternative groups. Without capping, the corresponding figures are about 99.0%, 97.1%, 98.3% and 93.0%. These are row-maximum proportions, not classification accuracies.

The broad structure is not completely overturned, but omitting Income changes the boundaries of Clusters 2 and 4 more noticeably. Removing capping also changes some assignments. Start with small segment-level pilots and clarify the income field before turning individual cluster labels into automatic decisions.

**Member 3 block ends here.**

**Start of responsibility block.**

## 4.1 Save and name the selected solution

Covered: W7 Exercise 4. Names reflect active-variable profiles, without inferring occupation, income source or retirement status. Numeric labels apply to this data, seed and preprocessing; review profiles before naming a changed solution.

```{r selected-clusters}
cluster_names <- c("Multi-product active", "Younger low-activity",
                   "Older low-activity", "Single-product active")
cluster_sizes <- data.frame(

)
cluster_sizes
```

Segment names: 1 Multi-product active; 2 Younger low-activity; 3 Older low-activity; 4 Single-product active.

## 4.2 Full profiles: every original variable

Covered: W7 Exercise 3. This table and the next chunk cover all seven variables: six numeric means and one category distribution. Use original Yield/CLV values.

```{r final-profiles}
cluster_means <- aggregate(bank_clustered[numeric_vars],
                           by = list(Cluster = bank_clustered$Cluster), FUN = mean)

cluster_profile

round(cluster_age_percent, 1)
```

Adapt W3 medians and W7 proportions. Positive mean Yield does not imply every customer in a segment is profitable. The mean of TRUE/FALSE values is a proportion.

```{r profile-risks}
cluster_medians <- aggregate(cbind(Yield, CLV) ~ Cluster, data = bank_clustered, FUN = median)
cluster_rates <- aggregate(
  data.frame(Loss_rate = bank_clustered$Loss_flag,

cluster_medians
cluster_rates
```

## 4.4 Compare current profit and recorded lifetime value

Use descriptive plots covered in the course. Keep the two scales separate: Yield and CLV do not necessarily refer to the same time horizon.

```{r profit-plots}
barplot(cluster_means$Yield, names.arg = cluster_means$Cluster,
        xlab = "Cluster", ylab = "Mean current Yield ($)", col = "steelblue")
barplot(cluster_means$CLV, names.arg = cluster_means$Cluster,
        xlab = "Cluster", ylab = "Mean recorded CLV ($)", col = "darkseagreen")
```

Covered: W7 scatterplots. A two-dimensional view cannot show every four-dimensional distance, so use it alongside silhouette scores and profiles.

```{r cluster-scatter}
plot(bank_clustered$Age, bank_clustered$No_Trans, col = bank_clustered$Cluster, pch = 16,

legend("topright", legend = paste("Cluster", 1:4), col = 1:4, pch = 16)
```

W7 also uses ANOVA and chi-square for profiling. Here, complete means/proportions and distributions form the main profile. # Member 5 — Predictive modelling

**Start of responsibility block.**


## 5.1 Receive the regression inputs from Member 1

Member 1 has already split training/validation records and prepared standardized_train. Fit the main model on original-value train_data and validate on validation_data. Only the coefficient-comparison model uses standardized_train. Check the inputs without repeating preparation.

```{r check-regression-inputs}
c(Training = nrow(train_data), Validation = nrow(validation_data))
stopifnot(nrow(standardized_train) == nrow(train_data))
stopifnot(!"Cluster" %in% names(train_data))
```

## 5.2 Why this model?

**Covered: W8 linear regression.** CLV is numeric. Use `CLV ~ Tot_Prod + No_Trans + Age` to explain conditional associations of relationship breadth, transaction activity and life stage with recorded CLV. Compared with W9 CART, a small regression is easier for a beginner to explain coefficient by coefficient and directly addresses Part 4's CLV-associated characteristics. CART is also permitted; this choice does not prove regression outperforms every tree.

Exclude Income because its zeros are ambiguous and it correlates strongly with the derived CLV label. Exclude Yield because it may enter the old formula and the objective is to understand customer characteristics. Exclude Cat_Age to avoid duplicated age information. Do not use full-data cluster labels as predictors. These are analytical choices for this assignment, not rules inherited from the earlier checklist.

For each predictor, H0: its coefficient is zero after controlling for the other two; H1: it is nonzero. For the overall F-test, H0: all three slopes are zero. Interpretation depends on model assumptions, which must be checked below.

Prediction here estimates the **existing CLV label** on records excluded from fitting. Without observed future profits, it does not validate actual future value.

## 5.3 Fit the model

Covered: W8 Exercise 2. Fit original-scale predictors; regression does not require scaling in the same way as distance-based clustering. Keep the complete summary in the appendix and present only key findings in the main slides.

```{r fit-regression}
clv_model <- lm(CLV ~ Tot_Prod + No_Trans + Age, data = train_data)
summary(clv_model)
```

## 5.4 Coefficients and confidence intervals

Coefficient interpretation is covered; exporting confidence intervals with confint is additional code. One additional product is associated with about $652 higher CLV, 100 transactions with about $495, and ten years of age with about $88, controlling for the other inputs. These are associations, not guaranteed gains.

```{r coefficients}
coefficient_table <- summary(clv_model)$coefficients
coefficient_table
confint(clv_model)
coef(clv_model)
```

## 5.5 Compare standardized coefficients

Covered concept: W8 slide 21 suggests standardized coefficients for relative importance. Member 1 has prepared standardized_train using scale; fit the comparison model with lm here. Raw coefficients 652 and 4.95 have different units and cannot be compared directly. This ranks associations only among included predictors.

```{r standardized-coefficients}
standardized_model <- lm(CLV ~ Tot_Prod + No_Trans + Age, data = standardized_train)
standardized_coefficients <- coef(standardized_model)[-1]
sort(abs(standardized_coefficients), decreasing = TRUE)
```

## 5.6 Check multicollinearity

VIF is covered in W8, where the lab uses car::vif. To avoid another package, use the equivalent base R formula 1/(1-R²), regressing each input on the other two. **This implementation is additional.** Values near one indicate little linear redundancy, not that all model assumptions hold.

```{r vif}
products_model <- lm(Tot_Prod ~ No_Trans + Age, data = train_data)
transactions_model <- lm(No_Trans ~ Tot_Prod + Age, data = train_data)
age_model <- lm(Age ~ Tot_Prod + No_Trans, data = train_data)
vif_values <- c(
  Tot_Prod = 1 / (1 - summary(products_model)$r.squared),
  No_Trans = 1 / (1 - summary(transactions_model)$r.squared),
  Age = 1 / (1 - summary(age_model)$r.squared)
)
vif_values
```

## 5.7 Residuals versus fitted

Covered: W8. Look for random scatter around zero, curvature and extreme residuals.

```{r diagnostic-1}
plot(clv_model, which = 1)
```

## 5.8 Normal Q-Q plot

Covered: W8. Large departures indicate non-normal residuals; predictors themselves need not be normally distributed.

```{r diagnostic-2}
plot(clv_model, which = 2)
```

## 5.9 Variance stability

Covered: W8. A trend or widening spread in Scale-Location raises concerns about equal variance.

```{r diagnostic-3}
plot(clv_model, which = 3)
```

## 5.10 Leverage and influence

Covered: W8. Inspect leverage and residual size. Labels are original row names, not customer IDs.

```{r diagnostic-5}
plot(clv_model, which = 5)
```

### Observed diagnostic findings

Training R² is about 0.494 and adjusted R² about 0.493. Conventional p-values for the three inputs are small. However, the Q-Q plot has a pronounced right-tail departure, there are very large positive residuals, and Scale-Location shows a trend. Normality and equal variance cannot be claimed. Interpret conventional standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals cautiously. Treat the model as an interpretable association baseline, not an unvalidated rule for individual treatment.

Standardized associations are approximately 0.565 for No_Trans, 0.281 for Tot_Prod and 0.112 for Age. Activity is strongest, followed by product breadth and age. Because Income/Yield were excluded, this is not an exhaustive ranking of all possible CLV drivers.

## 5.11 Additional: most influential observation sensitivity

W8 covers influence diagnostics; a leave-one-observation-out refit is additional sensitivity analysis. Temporarily omit the largest Cook-distance training observation to assess dependence on it. It is not proven erroneous and stays in the main model and raw data. Do not repeatedly choose deletions using validation results.

```{r influence-sensitivity}
cook_values <- cooks.distance(clv_model)
most_influential <- which.max(cook_values)
train_data[most_influential, ]
sensitivity_model <- lm(CLV ~ Tot_Prod + No_Trans + Age,
                        data = train_data[-most_influential, ])
cbind(Main = coef(clv_model), Without_one = coef(sensitivity_model))
```

The temporary exclusion is original row 2862, with CLV=$55,306 and Yield=$50,947. Coefficient signs remain unchanged and the transaction coefficient changes from about 4.95 to 4.84. The three directions are not generated solely by that observation; this does not resolve every influence concern.

## 5.12 Predict validation records

Adapted from W9 Exercise 2. Keep the model fixed and predict 3,000 records excluded from fitting. Do not delete or cap validation CLV outcomes.

```{r validation-predictions}
validation_prediction <- predict(clv_model, newdata = validation_data)
training_prediction <- predict(clv_model, newdata = train_data)
head(data.frame(Actual = validation_data$CLV, Predicted = validation_prediction))
```

## 5.13 RMSE and a simple baseline

RMSE is covered in W9. The mean baseline, MAE and validation R² are additional. The baseline predicts the training mean, not the validation mean. RMSE weights large errors more heavily; MAE is mean absolute error. Validation R² uses the validation mean in its denominator and may be negative.

```{r model-performance}
baseline_prediction <- rep(mean(train_data$CLV), nrow(validation_data))
performance <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Training regression", "Validation regression", "Validation mean baseline"),
  RMSE = c(sqrt(mean((train_data$CLV - training_prediction)^2)),
           sqrt(mean((validation_data$CLV - validation_prediction)^2)),
           sqrt(mean((validation_data$CLV - baseline_prediction)^2))),
  MAE = c(mean(abs(train_data$CLV - training_prediction)),
          mean(abs(validation_data$CLV - validation_prediction)),
          mean(abs(validation_data$CLV - baseline_prediction)))
)
performance
validation_r_squared <- 1 - sum((validation_data$CLV - validation_prediction)^2) /
  sum((validation_data$CLV - mean(validation_data$CLV))^2)
validation_r_squared
```

## 5.14 Actual versus predicted

Adapt a course scatterplot. The 45-degree line represents perfect prediction. Inspect high-value misses as well as average errors. The model may produce negative CLV predictions; do not silently replace them with zero.

```{r prediction-plot}
plot(validation_data$CLV, validation_prediction,
     xlab = "Actual recorded CLV", ylab = "Predicted CLV", pch = 16,
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2), main = "Validation predictions")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "red")
sum(validation_prediction < 0)
```

## 5.15 Prediction errors by age group

Additional check. Error is recorded CLV minus predicted CLV; a negative mean means overprediction of the existing label. Age-group errors cannot establish underestimation relative to true future profit.

```{r age-errors}
validation_errors <- data.frame(
  Age_group = as.character(validation_data$Under_30),
  Error = validation_data$CLV - validation_prediction,
  Absolute_error = abs(validation_data$CLV - validation_prediction))
aggregate(cbind(Error, Absolute_error) ~ Age_group, data = validation_errors, FUN = mean)
```

### Part 3 conclusions and limits

Validation RMSE is about $909 and MAE about $498, compared with mean-baseline RMSE about $1,360. Validation R² is about 0.551. The model estimates recorded CLV better than a constant mean on this split, but substantial errors remain. Lower validation than training error is possible because the training set happens to contain particularly extreme outcomes.

Mean error is about −$116 for younger customers and +$49 for others, indicating average overprediction of younger customers' existing labels. This is not independent evidence that the original formula undervalues them. Validation labels come from the same unknown formula. This is neither future-period validation nor verified independence of customer identities.

**Member 5 block ends here.**

# Member 6 — Business recommendations and final integration

**Start of responsibility block.**

## 6.1 Part 4: Turn findings into business recommendations

## 6.2 Summarize current-profit and recorded-CLV rankings

Covered: W7 profile interpretation and W9 Exercise 4 business synthesis. Rank the two outcomes separately rather than combining them into an undefined value score. Within-group variation warrants pilots.

```{r profit-ranking}
cluster_profile[order(-cluster_profile$Yield),
                c("Cluster", "Segment", "N", "Yield", "CLV")]
cluster_profile[order(-cluster_profile$CLV),
                c("Cluster", "Segment", "N", "Yield", "CLV")]
cluster_medians
cluster_rates
```

## 6.3 Executive interpretation

**Highest current profit:** Cluster 3, Older low-activity, with mean Yield about $282 and median $116. **Highest recorded CLV:** Cluster 1, Multi-product active, at about $3,234. Cluster 2, Younger low-activity, has the lowest means for both outcomes: Yield about $55 and CLV about $1,077, with about 57.9% currently loss-making. Cluster 4, Single-product active, has mean CLV about $2,644 but median Yield −$13 and about 53.2% currently loss-making.

Current profitability and the old formula's lifetime-value estimate are different. No segment has negative mean Yield, yet a majority of customers in some segments lose money currently. Present means alongside loss rates.

Transactions, product count and age all have positive conditional associations with recorded CLV, in descending standardized strength. These suggest pilots, not a claim that increasing transactions or selling one product causes $652 of extra profit.

## 6.4 Actions linked to both segments and model evidence

| Action | Segment and profile evidence | Model evidence and limit | Implementation and evaluation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pilot relevant cross-selling | Cluster 4: 1,855 customers, exactly one product each, about 409 transactions and $2,644 mean recorded CLV | Product coefficient about +$652; transactions have the strongest standardized association. These motivate needs research, not causal revenue estimates | Interview customers, then randomly invite a small eligible group. Compare acceptance, incremental net profit and complaints |
| Maintain active multi-product relationships | Cluster 1: 2,145 customers, 2.32 products and 397 transactions on average; highest mean CLV | Product breadth and activity are positively associated with CLV. There is no churn label, so this is not a high-churn-risk classification | Pilot service check-ins and relevant reminders. Track retention, service costs and actual profits; avoid blanket subsidies |
| Verify younger customers' income data and offer low-cost development support | Cluster 2: 3,347 customers; 44.2% under 30, 35.4% zero income, lower activity | Age has the weakest standardized association. The regression overpredicts younger customers' recorded labels by about $116 on average, so it cannot validate their true future potential | Clarify zero-income reasons and offer voluntary account-use support. Track subsequent actual profit, activity and fee burden; do not automatically raise fees or exclude low-CLV customers |
| Protect current profit and review service costs | Cluster 3: 2,653 customers, mean age about 69; highest mean current Yield but lower CLV | Age is a weaker model association than activity and product breadth. Low activity does not imply low current profit; the CLV model cannot replace Yield evidence | Pilot optional service channels and relationship support, without mechanical age-based pricing. Evaluate net profit, satisfaction and service costs |

Randomized pilots and incremental evaluation are **additional business-design suggestions**, not causal models already completed in this course analysis. The dataset lacks product-level holdings, churn, fees, service costs, tenure and future profit. It cannot support a specific product recommendation, churn probability or promised return.

## 6.5 Limitations and next steps

Request customer IDs, the Income definition and zero-value reasons, the old CLV formula/version history, product-level holdings, relationship duration, costs/fees, subsequent actual profits and churn. Clusters overlap and sensitivity choices may change assignments. Regression residuals violate ideal assumptions. Neither profiles nor coefficients establish causation. These limits distinguish useful exploratory evidence from a validated operating decision.

## 6.6 Part 5: A concrete ten-minute presentation plan

The complete assignment requests about 8–10 main slides followed by five minutes of Q&A. This ten-slide plan totals ten minutes: introduction one minute, exploration two, clustering two, prediction two, and recommendations/conclusion three. Present findings first and reserve managerial actions for the final section.

| Slide | Time | Title and message | Evidence / speaking points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1:00 | Which customers matter now and over the relationship? | Three business questions, 10,000 records and the analytical route; avoid jargon |
| 2 | 1:00 | Usable data, but zero income is ambiguous | 16.89% zero income; retain customers; adjust extreme distances only in the clustering copy |
| 3 | 1:00 | Lower recorded CLV for younger customers is not proof of underestimation | Compare CLV, income and activity; no observed future profit benchmark |
| 4 | 1:00 | Four customer relationship patterns | Names, sizes and active-variable profiles; explain k selection in one sentence |
| 5 | 1:00 | Current profit and recorded lifetime value rank differently | Yield/CLV means and loss rates: Cluster 3 leads current profit, Cluster 1 leads CLV |
| 6 | 1:00 | Activity and product breadth have the strongest CLV associations | Standardized ranking and exclusion rationale; no full R output on the main slide |
| 7 | 1:00 | Better than a mean guess, but not future-value validation | Validation RMSE $909 versus $1,360; extreme errors and unknown-formula limitation |
| 8 | 1:00 | Pilot cross-selling and relationship maintenance | Clusters 4 and 1, profile evidence, model evidence and pilot metrics |

Keep the main slides accessible to executives. Include necessary code and output in appendices, within the assignment's maximum of 50 appendix slides. Each notebook chunk does not need its own slide.

## 6.8 Prepare for Q&A

- **Why not two clusters?** Its score is higher, but it combines distinct age and product-breadth patterns. Four is an explicit business tradeoff.
- **Why retain outliers?** Genuine valuable customers may be extreme. Limit their distance influence and compare alternatives.
- **Why not CART?** Either method is permitted. A small regression explains conditional associations simply, with diagnostic weaknesses disclosed. A tree is a possible future comparison, not guaranteed to be better.
- **Are younger customers undervalued?** This cannot be established without actual future profit; existing-label differences are insufficient.
- **Does one more product create $652 profit?** No. That is a conditional association with recorded CLV. Incremental profit needs a pilot.
- **Why exclude Income/Yield?** They may mechanically enter the old formula, and Income has ambiguous zeros. The simpler explanation sacrifices information, and remaining inputs may also enter that formula.
